citations.quote:
Let $J$ be a nonempty compact interval and $n\ge1$. Continuous $\mathbb R^n$-valued curves on $J$ are complete in the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(x,y):=\sup_{t\in J}\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2.$$

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then
$$\lim_{r\to0^+}A_rf(x)=f(x)$$
for Lebesgue-almost every $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix an initial pair $(s,x_0)$ and a closed ball $K=\overline B(x_0,r)$. On a sufficiently short one-sided interval $J$ adjoining $s$, absolute continuity of the integrals of $m_K,L_K$ gives $\int_Jm_K\le r$ and $\int_JL_K<1$. On continuous curves taking values in $K$, define $\Phi(X)(t)=x_0+\int_s^t b(q,X(q))dq,$ with the oriented integral when J lies to the left of s. The integrand is measurable because $q\mapsto(q,X(q))$ is continuous and b is Borel; it is integrable because $|b(q,X(q))|\le m_K(q)$ almost everywhere. The map preserves the closed sup-norm ball of radius r about the constant curve $x_0$, and $\|\Phi(X)-\Phi(Y)\|_\infty\le(\int_JL_K)\|X-Y\|_\infty$. By [F1] it has a unique fixed point. The integral FTC [F2] makes this curve absolutely continuous and a solution almost everywhere.

If two solutions have the same value at one time and remain in a compact K on a common compact interval, partition that interval into finitely many subintervals on which $\int L_K<1$. On each subinterval beginning at a time where the solutions agree, their integral equations bound their sup-norm difference by $(\int L_K)$ times itself, so the difference is zero. Induction over the partition proves uniqueness throughout the common interval. Their union therefore defines a unique maximal solution. Suppose a maximal endpoint $\tau$ lies in $(0,T)$ and there are times $t_n\uparrow\tau$ with $X(t_n)$ in a compact set K. Choose R with K contained in the ball $B_R(0)$, put $K_1=\overline B_{R+1}(0)$, and take n large enough that $\int_{t_n}^{\tau}m_{K_1}<1$. If the path first reaches the boundary of $K_1$ at some $r\in(t_n,\tau)$, it stays in $K_1$ on $[t_n,r]$, so $|X(r)-X(t_n)|\le\int_{t_n}^r m_{K_1}<1$, while $|X(r)-X(t_n)|\ge |X(r)|-|X(t_n)|\ge1$, a contradiction. Thus it stays in $K_1$ up to $\tau$; the same integrable bound makes it Cauchy there, and its finite limit lets step 1.1 extend it past $\tau$, again a contradiction. Hence no compact set contains trajectory values at times arbitrarily close to an interior maximal endpoint: the path eventually leaves every compact set.

Assume the spatial derivative hypothesis. On a short interval and compact ball as in step 1.1, solutions from nearby initial points remain in a common compact ball. The contraction estimate gives $\|X(\cdot;s,x_0+h)-X(\cdot;s,x_0)\|_\infty\le C|h|$. Write $\Delta_h(t)=X(t;s,x_0+h)-X(t;s,x_0)$. The state-variable fundamental theorem of calculus [F3] gives $\Delta_h(t)=h+\int_s^t A_h(q)\Delta_h(q)dq,\quad A_h(q)=\int_0^1D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0)+\theta\Delta_h(q))d\theta.$ Put $A(q)=D_xb(q,X(q;s,x_0))$ at the almost-everywhere times where the spatial differential exists, with value zero on its exceptional time set. The matrix equation $V(t)=I_d+\int_s^tA(q)V(q)dq$ has a unique continuous solution by the contraction argument of step 1.1, since $\int_JL_K<1$. Subtracting its product with h from the equation for $\Delta_h$ gives $\Delta_h(t)-V(t)h=\int_s^t A_h(q)(\Delta_h(q)-V(q)h)dq+\int_s^t(A_h(q)-A(q))V(q)h\,dq.$ Taking sup norms and absorbing the first term bounds the left side by $C|h|\int_J\|A_h-A\|dq=o(|h|)$. Thus $D_{x_0}X=V$; dominated convergence in the same integral equation proves continuity of V in $x_0$. The integral FTC [F2] yields $\dot V=A(t)V$ almost everywhere. Repeating on a finite cover by overlapping short intervals gives $C^1$ dependence throughout each common flow domain and continuous dependence in the uniform path norm on trajectories existing through the full interval.

Uniqueness makes the time map from s to t injective. Continuous dependence makes its domain open; solving backward from time t shows its image is open and its inverse is the backward flow, which is $C^1$ by step 3.1. The chain rule [F5] says the derivative of the inverse times V is the identity. Thus the time map is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism between its open domain and image.

Fix a compact flow tube and a compact set K of states it visits. For a fixed target time t, choose a compact time interval J containing t and the varying start times, with all trajectories in the flow identity remaining in K. For trajectories with the same starting time, the integral equation gives $|X(r;s,y)-X(r;s,z)|\le|y-z|+\int_JL_K(q)|X(q;s,y)-X(q;s,z)|dq$; iterating this inequality yields the spatial Lipschitz bound $|X(t;s,y)-X(t;s,z)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}|y-z|$. For $s,s+h\in J$, the flow identity and the integral equation along the short backward segment give $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and $|X(s;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$, where the integral is over the unoriented interval. Hence $|X(t;s+h,x)-X(t;s,x)|\le e^{\int_JL_K}\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K(q)dq$. Summing over any disjoint adjacent intervals shows that $s\mapsto X(t;s,x)$ is locally absolutely continuous, uniformly for x in the tube. To identify its derivative, choose a countable dense subset Q of K. By [F6], outside one null set the functions $m_K,L_K$ and $s\mapsto b(s,q)$ for all $q\in Q$ have their values as limits of local averages; also the spatial Lipschitz bound holds at such s. Approximation by q and the common Lipschitz bound show that the averages of $b(r,x)$ over intervals shrinking to s converge to $b(s,x)$ uniformly for $x\in K$. For the solution started at x at time $s+h$, the magnitude bound gives $|X(r;s+h,x)-x|\le\int_{[s,s+h]}m_K=O(|h|)$ uniformly between s and s+h at these Lebesgue points. Replacing $b(r,x)$ by $b(r,X(r;s+h,x))$ in the average contributes at most $|h|^{-1}O(|h|)\int_{[s,s+h]}L_K(r)dr=O(|h|)$. The integral equation therefore gives $[X(s;s+h,x)-x]/h\to-b(s,x)$ uniformly on K. The flow identity $X(t;s+h,x)=X(t;s,X(s;s+h,x))$ and the spatial derivative from step 3.1 yield $\partial_sX(t;s,x)=-D_xX(t;s,x)b(s,x)$ almost everywhere on the tube. The right side has the integrable local bound $e^{\int_JL_K}m_K(s)$, consistent with and also giving the local absolute continuity.

boundaries.evidence: The initial point is prescribed. Step 1.1 performs contraction on a closed ball of continuous curves that contains the constant path at that point, so the fixed-point domain cannot be empty; if an empty compact state set is considered, its local bounds are merely vacuous.

boundaries.evidence: For b identically zero, the integral map in step 1.1 is the constant path x0. The resulting flow is stationary, with spatial derivative the identity in step 3.1; zero magnitude and Lipschitz bounds require no division.

boundaries.evidence: When d=1 the integral equation in step 1.1 is scalar and the matrix variational equation in step 3.1 has one entry with initial value one. The same short-interval contraction and inverse-flow argument apply.

boundaries.evidence: A spatially constant time-integrable field has Lipschitz bound zero. Its solution is the explicit time integral added to the initial point, and step 3.1 gives an identity spatial derivative, so lack of spatial variation causes no flow singularity.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 uses a one-sided interval when the initial time is a boundary time. Step 2.1 restricts the escape alternative to maximal endpoints strictly inside the time horizon; no endpoint differentiability or terminal probability law is asserted by this ODE lemma.

boundaries.evidence: Statement and proof preserve the stated axiom branch: Countable Choice is used only through the scalar Lebesgue FTC to identify derivatives of time integrals; the contraction and flow construction make no further choice. Its construction begins in step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The contraction constructs a unique maximal solution, and the additional spatial differential hypothesis gives flow regularity. These are existence and regularity conclusions, not a characterization making the integral bounds necessary for every uniquely solvable vector field.

risk_review.notes: Contraction on a closed ball uses integrals of m_K and L_K smaller than radius and one. The reader return-sequence annulus estimate forces eventual compact escape; time reversal gives the left endpoint case. Matrix difference quotients are controlled by integrable local derivative bounds; uniqueness gives inverse flows. A countable dense set and Lebesgue differentiation give the simultaneous-in-x starting-time derivative on compact tubes. Checked current cited supplier interfaces, quantifiers, zero/endpoint cases and exact choice assumptions. Citation repairs do not change the mathematical interface.
